entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Fixed so firmly in a person's mind or in a group's way of life that it is very hard to change or remove.
entries.usage: Used for habits, attitudes, beliefs, fears and cultural patterns, and very often with *deeply* or *so*: *a deeply ingrained habit*. The usual preposition is *in*: *ingrained in our culture*, *ingrained in him from childhood*. It is neutral and works in conversation and writing; the spelling *engrained* also exists but is less common.
entries.pattern: deeply ingrained (in someone / something); an ingrained habit / belief / attitude
examples: Saying “sorry” when someone bumps into me is so **ingrained** that I do it without thinking.
My grandmother's habit of saving every jar and rubber band was **ingrained** during the Depression.
A culture of very long hours is deeply **ingrained** in the legal profession.

drill.sentence: Checking her phone the minute she wakes up is a deeply {{ingrained}} habit that she's trying to break.
drill.hint: fixed so firmly it's hard to change (not *rooted* or *entrenched*)

entries.related: *entrenched* — firmly established, often about systems and positions; *deep-rooted* — similar, about feelings and problems; *innate* — present from birth, not learned.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A right or privilege that belongs to a particular person or group because of who they are or the role they have.
entries.usage: In conversation it appears mostly in *it's your prerogative (to do something)*, said when you accept someone's choice even if you don't like it. In formal writing it describes the powers of an office: *the prerogative of the court*, *a management prerogative*. Note the spelling *pre-*: many Americans pronounce the first syllable *per-*, and the misspelling *perogative* is common.
entries.pattern: it's someone's prerogative (to do something); the prerogative of + person / group
examples: If you'd rather skip the wedding, that's your **prerogative**, but Mom will be hurt.
Hiring decisions are the manager's **prerogative**, not HR's.
The judge reminded the jury that setting the sentence was the court's **prerogative**.

drill.sentence: You don't have to explain why you left the party early; it's your {{prerogative}}.
drill.hint: yours alone to decide, formal word (not *choice*, *call*, *right* or *privilege*)

entries.related: *right* — more general, often legal; *privilege* — a special advantage, not always tied to a role; *discretion* — freedom to decide (*at the manager's discretion*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Extremely upsetting and frightening to go through, to watch or to hear about.
entries.usage: Common in news, reviews and personal stories about disasters, accidents, crime and serious illness: *a harrowing ordeal*, *a harrowing escape*, *harrowing footage*. It describes experiences and accounts of them, not people, and it is much stronger than *upsetting*. Most Americans say HAIR-oh-ing (*marry* sounds like *merry*); many in the Northeast keep the vowel of *cat*.
entries.pattern: a harrowing experience / ordeal / escape / account / story
examples: The survivors gave a **harrowing** account of the night the dam broke.
Getting three kids through airport security on my own was a **harrowing** experience.
The documentary includes **harrowing** footage of families escaping the wildfire.

drill.sentence: After forty hours stuck on a mountain ledge, the climbers described their {{harrowing}} ordeal to reporters.
drill.hint: deeply distressing and frightening (not *terrifying*, *traumatic*, *horrific* or *grueling*)

entries.related: *traumatic* — causing lasting psychological harm; *grueling* — exhausting rather than frightening; *hair-raising* — informal, frightening in an exciting way.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A strong liking for something, or a habit of doing it, often something a little unusual or excessive.
entries.usage: Almost always *a penchant for* + noun or *-ing*: *a penchant for expensive shoes*, *a penchant for exaggerating*. It is often mildly humorous or critical, and it is common in journalism and educated speech; in casual talk people say *a thing for* or *a weakness for*. Americans say PEN-chunt; the French-style pronunciation is mainly British.
entries.pattern: a penchant for + noun / -ing
examples: My uncle has a **penchant** for loud Hawaiian shirts, even at funerals.
She's always had a **penchant** for vintage clothes and old jazz records.
The CEO's **penchant** for bold promises has started to make investors nervous.

drill.sentence: My sister has a {{penchant}} for dramatic exits; she never just leaves a party, she announces it.
drill.hint: a habitual liking, often an odd one (not *fondness*, *flair* or *passion*)

entries.related: *propensity* — a natural tendency, often toward bad behavior, more formal; *predilection* — a preference, more formal; *knack* — a natural skill.

entries.label: adverb / adjective
entries.meaning: In exactly the same words as were originally said or written; word for word.
entries.usage: As an adverb it usually comes after the verb and its object: *quote / copy / repeat something verbatim*. As an adjective it goes before a noun: *a verbatim transcript*, *a verbatim quote*. It is common in journalism, law and school contexts such as plagiarism, and also in everyday talk about what someone said.
entries.pattern: quote / copy / repeat something verbatim; a verbatim transcript / record / quote
examples: The student copied two whole paragraphs **verbatim** from Wikipedia and didn't cite them.
I can't remember her words **verbatim**, but she basically called me lazy.
The court released a **verbatim** transcript of the hearing on Friday.

drill.sentence: He didn't bother to rewrite the press release; he just pasted it {{verbatim}} into his blog post.
drill.hint: using exactly the original wording (one word, not *as is* or *directly*)

entries.related: *word for word* — same meaning, more conversational; *paraphrase* — the opposite, say the same thing in your own words; *literally* — in the literal sense, a different word.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To stop someone from doing what they planned, or to stop a plan or attempt from succeeding.
entries.usage: Common in news about crime, security and competition: *thwart a robbery*, *thwart an attack*, *thwart someone's plans*. It is very often passive: *the plot was thwarted*. For small everyday problems it sounds dramatic, so people use it there mainly as a joke.
entries.pattern: thwart a plan / attempt / attack; be thwarted by something
examples: Quick-thinking bank staff **thwarted** an attempted robbery on Main Street yesterday.
Our plans for a picnic were **thwarted** by a sudden thunderstorm.
Two-factor authentication can **thwart** most attempts to break into your email account.

drill.sentence: Every time the squirrel tried to reach the bird feeder, the metal cone on the pole {{thwarted}} it.
drill.hint: prevented it from succeeding (not *foiled*, *stopped* or *blocked*)

entries.related: *foil* — very close, common in crime news; *frustrate* — prevent plans from succeeding, more formal; *derail* — knock a plan off course.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To ask for something such as feedback, money, opinions or offers, usually in a formal way or from many people.
entries.usage: Common in business, nonprofit and government contexts: *solicit feedback / input / donations / bids / proposals*. It sounds formal; in conversation, *ask for* is more natural. Always give the object: used alone, *solicit* suggests selling door to door (the *No Soliciting* signs on American doors) or offering sex for money.
entries.pattern: solicit feedback / input / donations / bids (from someone)
examples: The city is **soliciting** input from residents on the design of the new park.
Volunteers went door to door **soliciting** donations for the food bank.
We're **soliciting** feedback from early users before the full launch of the app.

drill.sentence: Before replacing the roof, the condo board {{solicited}} bids from five different contractors.
drill.hint: formally asked for (not *requested*, *sought* or *invited*)

entries.related: *request* — ask formally for one specific thing; *seek* — try to get, formal; *canvass* — ask many people for their opinions or votes.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To stop resisting something stronger, such as pressure, temptation or illness; *succumb to* an illness or injuries can also mean to die of it.
entries.usage: The thing you give in to follows *to*: *succumb to pressure / temptation / exhaustion*. In news, *succumbed to his injuries* is a standard, respectful way to report a death. In casual talk it sounds playfully dramatic (*I finally succumbed and bought the bigger TV*), and it can stand alone when the context is clear.
entries.pattern: succumb to pressure / temptation / an illness / injuries
examples: After a week of saying no, I **succumbed** to the kids' begging and bought a puppy.
The driver **succumbed** to his injuries two days after the crash.
Under pressure from shareholders, the board finally **succumbed** and replaced the CEO.

drill.sentence: I was doing so well on my diet until Friday, when I {{succumbed}} to a box of donuts in the break room.
drill.hint: stopped resisting (formal, not *gave in*, *yielded* or *surrendered*)

mistake.wrong: She finally succumbed the pressure and resigned.
mistake.right: She finally succumbed to the pressure and resigned.
mistake.why: *Succumb* takes no direct object; the thing you give in to needs *to*.

entries.related: *give in (to)* — the everyday equivalent; *yield to* — formal, also used for traffic; *resist* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Harmless, and not likely to offend or upset anyone.
entries.usage: Often used for remarks, questions, messages and substances: *an innocuous comment*, *an innocuous question*. It is very frequent with *seemingly*, when something harmless-looking turns out to cause trouble. It is a little formal; in everyday talk, *harmless* is more usual.
entries.pattern: a (seemingly) innocuous remark / question / comment / message
examples: A seemingly **innocuous** question about her ex turned dinner into a two-hour argument.
Most of the spiders you find in your house are completely **innocuous**.
The text looked **innocuous**, but the link in it led to a fake bank website.

drill.sentence: His joke seemed {{innocuous}} enough, but a few people at the table clearly felt insulted.
drill.hint: unlikely to offend anyone (formal, not *harmless*, *innocent* or *inoffensive*)

entries.related: *harmless* — the everyday word; *inoffensive* — not offensive, sometimes meaning dull; *insidious* — harmful in a hidden, gradual way.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Acceptable, or easy enough to agree to, even if it is not ideal.
entries.usage: Mostly used for ideas, offers, plans and choices, often in the comparative: *a more palatable option*, *make the cuts more palatable to voters*. The person who accepts it follows *to*. The literal sense, pleasant to eat, exists but is less common, and the opposite *unpalatable* is frequent in *an unpalatable truth*.
entries.pattern: palatable to someone; make something more palatable
examples: Splitting the cost into twelve monthly payments made the price much more **palatable**.
The union found the new offer far more **palatable** than the first one.
None of the options for the old bridge are **palatable**: close it for a year or pay twice as much.

drill.sentence: To make the rent increase more {{palatable}}, the landlord offered to repaint the whole apartment.
drill.hint: easier to accept (not *acceptable*, *tolerable* or *bearable*)

entries.related: *acceptable* — plainer; *tolerable* — just bearable; *unpalatable* — the opposite, hard to accept.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Old-fashioned and no longer suited to modern needs or conditions.
entries.usage: Critical; used for laws, rules, systems, equipment and attitudes: *antiquated laws*, *an antiquated computer system*. It suggests that the thing should have been replaced long ago. For old things that are valued, use *antique* or *vintage* instead.
entries.pattern: antiquated laws / rules / equipment / systems / ideas
examples: The airline blamed the delays on an **antiquated** scheduling system that crashed during the storm.
My grandfather has some pretty **antiquated** ideas about who should do the dishes.
The town finally got rid of an **antiquated** rule that banned dancing in bars after midnight.

drill.sentence: The house is charming, but its {{antiquated}} wiring would never pass a modern safety inspection.
drill.hint: so old it no longer meets today's standards (not *outdated*, *obsolete*, *ancient* or *aging*)

entries.related: *outdated* — plainer, more neutral; *obsolete* — no longer used at all; *antique* — old and valuable (furniture, jewelry).

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who regularly gives opinions about a subject, such as politics or sports, in the media.
entries.usage: Common in talk about TV, radio and online commentary: *political pundits*, *sports pundits*, *cable news pundits*. It often sounds slightly dismissive, suggesting people who speak confidently but are often wrong (*the pundits got it wrong again*). In British English it is also the neutral word for a TV soccer analyst.
entries.pattern: political / sports / TV pundits; pundits predicted / argued that …
examples: Most **pundits** picked the home team to win easily, but they lost by twenty points.
Every Sunday morning, the same **pundits** argue about the same issues on TV.
My brother watches so much football that he talks like a TV **pundit**.

drill.sentence: After the surprise result, the {{pundits}} who had called it a sure thing were suddenly very quiet.
drill.hint: people paid to give opinions in the media (not *experts*, *analysts*, *pollsters* or *commentators*)

entries.related: *commentator* — more neutral; *talking head* — informal and dismissive, someone who appears on TV to give opinions; *analyst* — suggests expertise and data.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make a process or action happen more quickly than usual.
entries.usage: Typical of business, government and customer service: *expedite the process / an application / a refund / delivery*. Americans see it constantly in *expedited shipping* when shopping online and *expedited service* for passports. In conversation, *speed up* or *rush* is more natural.
entries.pattern: expedite a process / application / delivery; expedited shipping / service
examples: I paid an extra sixty dollars to **expedite** my passport renewal before the trip.
We chose **expedited** shipping so the gift would arrive before Christmas.
The new rule is meant to **expedite** permits for small housing projects.

drill.sentence: Could you {{expedite}} my refund? I need the money to pay rent next week.
drill.hint: make it happen faster (formal, not *speed up* or *rush*)

entries.related: *speed up* — the everyday phrase; *fast-track* — give something priority; *accelerate* — increase speed, more about rates and growth.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Extremely complicated and difficult to follow, usually more than it needs to be.
entries.usage: Critical; used for explanations, arguments, rules, processes and plots: *a convoluted explanation*, *a convoluted plot*, *convoluted tax rules*. It implies that the complexity is unnecessary or badly organized, not just that the subject is hard. Common in both speech and writing.
entries.pattern: a convoluted explanation / process / plot / argument / system
examples: By season four, the show's plot was so **convoluted** that I needed a chart to keep track of who was related to whom.
Getting reimbursed for travel involves a **convoluted** process with four forms and two signatures.
He gave a long, **convoluted** excuse about why he couldn't come to the wedding.

drill.sentence: The instructions for the bookcase were so {{convoluted}} that I gave up and watched a video instead.
drill.hint: so twisted they're hard to follow (not *complicated*, *complex*, *confusing* or *cryptic*)

entries.related: *complicated* — plainer, can be neutral; *byzantine* — extremely complicated, often about bureaucracy; *straightforward* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The most important or central point of a problem, argument or issue, the one that decides everything else.
entries.usage: Almost always *the crux of* + noun: *the crux of the matter / problem / argument / issue*. It is common in writing and educated speech, often when you want to move past side details (*the crux of it is …*). It is nearly always singular.
entries.pattern: the crux of the matter / problem / issue / argument
examples: The **crux** of the problem is that nobody knows who actually owns the fence.
Cost is the **crux** of the debate over the new stadium.
Let's skip the details and get to the **crux** of it: can we afford this house or not?

drill.sentence: They argued for an hour about dishes and laundry, but the {{crux}} of the issue was that she felt unappreciated.
drill.hint: the central, deciding point (one short word, not *heart*, *core* or *root*)

entries.related: *the heart of the matter* — same idea, more conversational; *gist* — the general meaning, not the deciding point; *nub* — informal, the central point.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A first, short or experimental attempt at an activity or field that is new for you.
entries.usage: Usually *a foray into* + field, often with *first*, *brief* or *unsuccessful*: *her first foray into politics*. It is common in journalism and business writing about people and companies trying something new, and it sounds lightly humorous in conversation. The original sense, a short military raid, is now much less common.
entries.pattern: (someone's first / brief) foray into + activity or field
examples: The singer's first **foray** into acting got terrible reviews.
Our brief **foray** into backyard chickens ended when a raccoon got into the coop.
The company's **foray** into the restaurant business lost millions in its first year.

drill.sentence: After his disastrous {{foray}} into online dating, he decided to let his friends set him up instead.
drill.hint: brief first attempt at something new (not *venture*)

entries.related: *venture* — a risky new project, often in business; *dabble in* — do something casually, without commitment; *raid* — a sudden attack, close to the original military sense.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Being the most typical or perfect example of a particular kind of person or thing.
entries.usage: Usually before a noun with *the*: *the quintessential New York deli*, *the quintessential American road trip*. It is common in journalism, travel writing and reviews, and in educated conversation. The adverb *quintessentially* is also frequent, especially with nationalities: *quintessentially American*.
entries.pattern: the quintessential + noun; quintessentially + adjective
examples: For many people, driving Route 66 is the **quintessential** American road trip.
With her clipboard and color-coded calendar, she's the **quintessential** soccer mom.
The diner served the **quintessential** small-town breakfast: eggs, hash browns and endless coffee.

drill.sentence: Rain, gray skies and a cup of tea by the window: it was the {{quintessential}} London afternoon.
drill.hint: being the purest example of (not *classic*, *typical*, *ultimate* or *iconic*)

entries.related: *classic* — typical and well known, more casual; *archetypal* — the original model of a type, more formal; *epitome* — the noun, *the epitome of*.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Worried or slightly afraid that something bad or unpleasant is going to happen.
entries.usage: Milder and a little more formal than *scared*; it describes nervousness before an event: *apprehensive about the surgery*, *apprehensive about starting a new job*. The usual pattern is *apprehensive about* + noun or *-ing*. Common in both speech and writing.
entries.pattern: be / feel apprehensive about something / about doing something
examples: I was a little **apprehensive** about meeting her parents for the first time.
Many homeowners are **apprehensive** about the new flood maps, which could raise their insurance costs.
The dog looked **apprehensive** as the vet walked toward him with a needle.

drill.sentence: She felt {{apprehensive}} before her first solo flight, but the landing went perfectly.
drill.hint: worried something might go wrong (not *nervous*, *anxious*, *afraid* or *uneasy*)

entries.related: *nervous* — the everyday word; *anxious* — stronger, often more lasting; *wary* — careful because of possible danger.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Continuing without stopping, in a way that is annoying or unpleasant.
entries.usage: Almost always negative, and used for noises, talk, demands and bad weather: *incessant barking*, *incessant chatter*, *incessant questions*, *incessant rain*. It usually goes before the noun. The adverb is common too: *he talks incessantly*.
entries.pattern: incessant noise / barking / chatter / rain / demands; talk incessantly
examples: The **incessant** barking from next door kept us up all night.
After a week of **incessant** rain, the river finally flooded the park.
I love my nephew, but his **incessant** questions wear me out by dinnertime.

drill.sentence: I couldn't focus on my book because of the {{incessant}} drilling from the construction site across the street.
drill.hint: never stopping, and annoying (not *constant*, *nonstop* or *endless*)

entries.related: *constant* — more neutral; *relentless* — never weakening, can be positive (*relentless effort*); *intermittent* — the opposite, stopping and starting.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Shocking or unpleasant because it is sudden, out of place or does not fit with what is around it.
entries.usage: Used for changes, contrasts, sounds, colors and transitions: *a jarring contrast*, *a jarring transition*, *a jarring note*. It is common in reviews, design talk and conversation. A frequent pattern is *it's jarring to* + verb: *It's jarring to see your hometown on the news*.
entries.pattern: a jarring contrast / change / transition / note; it's jarring to see / hear something
examples: Going from a week of quiet in the mountains back to Manhattan traffic was **jarring**.
The movie's sudden switch from comedy to horror felt **jarring** rather than clever.
It's always **jarring** to hear your own voice on a recording.

drill.sentence: The bright orange sofa looks {{jarring}} in a living room that's otherwise all soft grays and whites.
drill.hint: clashing in a sudden, unpleasant way (not *garish* or *odd*)

entries.related: *incongruous* — out of place, more formal; *grating* — irritating, mostly about sounds and voices; *jolting* — shaking, more physical.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A particular point in time or in a process, especially an important one when a decision has to be made.
entries.usage: Mostly in fixed phrases: *at this juncture* and *a critical / crucial / pivotal juncture*. *At this juncture* is common in official statements, law and business, but in conversation it can sound pompous; *at this point* or *right now* is more natural.
entries.pattern: at this / that juncture; at a critical / crucial juncture
examples: The team is at a critical **juncture**: if they lose tonight, the season is over.
At this **juncture**, the company has no plans to close its Denver office.
The talks have reached a delicate **juncture**, and neither side is commenting.

drill.sentence: “I can't comment on the cause of the fire at this {{juncture}},” the fire chief told reporters.
drill.hint: particular moment in a process (formal, not *point*, *time*, *stage* or *moment*)

entries.related: *point* — the everyday word (*at this point*); *crossroads* — a moment when you must choose a direction; *turning point* — when things change decisively.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In a completely clear and certain way, leaving no doubt and allowing no exceptions.
entries.usage: Strongly tied to denials and refusals: *categorically deny*, *categorically reject*, *categorically refuse*, *categorically rule out*. It is very common in official statements and press releases. In conversation it sounds emphatic and formal, which can be useful when you want to leave no room for doubt.
entries.pattern: categorically deny / reject / refuse / rule out something
examples: The company **categorically** denies that it knew about the safety problem.
My mother **categorically** refused to move into assisted living.
The coach **categorically** ruled out a return to the team next season.

drill.sentence: The landlord {{categorically}} rejected our request to get a cat, so we're looking for a new apartment.
drill.hint: without any qualification or doubt (not *flatly*, *firmly*, *curtly* or *emphatically*)

entries.related: *flatly* — similar, a little less formal; *unequivocally* — completely clearly; *emphatically* — with strong emphasis.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not committed to any particular option, method or view, and open to whichever one works best.
entries.usage: A figurative use that is common in tech, business and policy talk: *agnostic about the tools*, *platform-agnostic*, *vendor-agnostic*. It also takes *on* (*agnostic on the question*). It sounds analytical, a little jargony in casual talk, and is different from the religious sense (unsure whether God exists).
entries.pattern: agnostic about / on something; platform-agnostic, vendor-agnostic
examples: I'm totally **agnostic** about where we eat tonight, as long as there's parking.
The new framework is hardware-**agnostic**, so it runs on GPUs or ordinary CPUs.
The school board says it's **agnostic** about which bus company it uses, as long as the buses run on time.

drill.sentence: I'm fairly {{agnostic}} about whether we rent or buy; I just want to live closer to my parents.
drill.hint: not committed either way (not *neutral*, *indifferent*, *ambivalent* or *undecided*)

entries.related: *neutral* — not taking sides; *indifferent* — not caring; *open-minded* — willing to consider new ideas.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Using only a small amount of something, or doing something only rarely, because it should not be overused.
entries.usage: Common in instructions, recipes, medical advice and writing advice: *use sparingly*, *apply sparingly*, *eat red meat sparingly*. It usually comes after the verb and its object. The adjective appears in *be sparing with* (*be sparing with the salt*).
entries.pattern: use / apply / eat something sparingly; be sparing with something
examples: This hot sauce is extremely strong, so use it **sparingly**.
The doctor told him to apply the steroid cream **sparingly**, only on the worst patches.
Good writers use exclamation points **sparingly**.

drill.sentence: Water is so scarce on the island that residents use it {{sparingly}} and reuse bathwater for the garden.
drill.hint: only in small amounts (not *carefully*, *wisely* or *frugally*)

entries.related: *in moderation* — not too much, often about food and drink; *frugally* — spending little money; *liberally* — the opposite, in large amounts.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A team, department or system that works in isolation from others and does not share information with them.
entries.usage: Business and management language, almost always critical: *work in silos*, *break down silos*. The adjective *siloed* is common too (*siloed teams*, *siloed data*). Outside the office it can sound like a corporate buzzword.
entries.pattern: work / operate in silos; break down (the) silos; siloed teams / data
examples: Our sales and support teams work in **silos**, so customers have to explain their problem twice.
The new mayor promised to break down the **silos** between the city's housing and health departments.
When each hospital keeps records in its own **silo**, doctors can't see a patient's full history.

drill.sentence: At our kids' school, the math and science teachers work in {{silos}} and rarely plan lessons together.
drill.hint: separate units cut off from each other (not *isolation*)

entries.related: *siloed* — the adjective, isolated; *fiefdom* — a department run by one person who resists outsiders; *cross-functional* — involving several departments, the opposite idea.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Impossible to defend against criticism, or impossible to continue or maintain.
entries.usage: Used for positions, arguments and situations: *an untenable position*, *the situation became untenable*. It is common in news, law and business, often to explain why someone resigned or why a plan was dropped. In conversation, *impossible* or *can't go on like this* is more natural.
entries.pattern: an untenable position / situation / argument; become untenable
examples: With two roommates who never cleaned, the situation became **untenable**, so I moved out.
After the emails leaked, the coach's position was **untenable**, and he resigned the next day.
Given the new safety data, the claim that the drug has no side effects is **untenable**.

drill.sentence: Commuting three hours each way was {{untenable}} with a newborn, so they moved closer to the city.
drill.hint: no longer possible to keep up (formal; not *unsustainable*, *unbearable* or *unworkable*)

entries.related: *indefensible* — impossible to defend, often morally; *unsustainable* — cannot continue at the same rate; *tenable* — the opposite, often in *no longer tenable*.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Much higher than is reasonable or fair; used about prices, fees, costs and demands.
entries.usage: Strongly critical; it goes with *prices*, *fees*, *rent*, *interest rates* and *cost*. It is used in conversation, complaints and news. Note the spelling: there is no *h* after the *x*.
entries.pattern: exorbitant prices / fees / rent / interest rates
examples: The hotel charged an **exorbitant** fee for parking: forty-five dollars a night.
Many young families can't afford the **exorbitant** cost of daycare in big cities.
Payday lenders often charge **exorbitant** interest rates to people with no other options.

drill.sentence: We skipped the airport restaurant because of its {{exorbitant}} prices: twelve dollars for a bottle of water.
drill.hint: unreasonably high (not *outrageous*, *inflated*, *steep* or *extortionate*)

entries.related: *steep* — informal, quite high; *extortionate* — even stronger, more common in British English; *reasonable* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very detailed, broken down into small and specific parts.
entries.usage: Business, tech and data language: *granular data*, *granular control*, *at a granular level*. *Let's get more granular* is common in meetings, but in casual conversation it can sound like jargon. The literal sense is *made of small grains*.
entries.pattern: granular data / detail / control; at a granular level; get (more) granular
examples: The app gives parents **granular** control over which websites their kids can visit.
My sister planned her wedding day in **granular** detail, down to five-minute slots.
We need more **granular** sales numbers to see which stores are actually losing money.

drill.sentence: The new electric bills are much more {{granular}}: they show how much power you used every hour.
drill.hint: broken down into fine detail (not *detailed* or *specific*)

entries.related: *detailed* — the everyday word; *fine-grained* — the same idea, common in technical writing; *high-level* — the opposite, general.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In a way that cannot be explained or understood.
entries.usage: Common in news, stories and conversation to report something strange, often with surprise or mild frustration: *inexplicably disappeared*, *inexplicably popular*. It goes before the verb or adjective, or at the start of a sentence as a comment: *Inexplicably, the store closed in December*. Some Americans stress the second syllable, in-EK-splik-uh-blee.
entries.pattern: inexplicably + verb / adjective; Inexplicably, + clause
examples: After a week of searching, my keys **inexplicably** turned up in the freezer.
**Inexplicably**, the best restaurant on our street is always empty, while the mediocre one next door has a line.
The show was **inexplicably** canceled right after its best season.

drill.sentence: My grandmother's cat, who hates everyone, {{inexplicably}} adores our new neighbor.
drill.hint: for no reason anyone can explain (not *mysteriously*, *strangely* or *somehow*)

entries.related: *mysteriously* — similar, suggests something hidden; *unaccountably* — formal, the same meaning; *understandably* — the opposite idea.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To gradually make someone have a feeling, attitude or value, through teaching, example or experience.
entries.usage: Common with parents, teachers and coaches: *instill confidence / discipline / values / a love of reading*. The standard pattern is *instill something in someone*; *instill someone with something* also occurs, but many editors prefer the first. *Instill* is the American spelling; British English writes *instil*.
entries.pattern: instill something (confidence, discipline, values) in someone
examples: My grandfather **instilled** in me a love of fishing and a lot of patience.
Good coaches **instill** discipline without making practice miserable.
The program tries to **instill** good money habits in teenagers before they get a credit card.

drill.sentence: My parents tried to {{instill}} good manners in us by making us write thank-you notes after every birthday.
drill.hint: gradually build into someone's character (not *foster*, *ingrain* or *inculcate*)

entries.related: *inculcate* — very formal, teach by repetition; *foster* — encourage something to develop; *ingrain* — fix deeply, mostly as *ingrained*.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To stop something from developing or from being expressed, such as creativity, growth, a yawn or a laugh.
entries.usage: Two common uses: stopping development (*stifle innovation / competition / creativity / debate*), which is frequent and critical in business and policy, and holding back a reaction (*stifle a yawn / a laugh*). The adjective *stifling* usually means hot and airless (*a stifling room*) or oppressive.
entries.pattern: stifle innovation / creativity / growth / debate; stifle a yawn / laugh
examples: I had to **stifle** a laugh when the groom's phone rang during the vows.
Critics say the new rules will **stifle** competition among small airlines.
Constant deadlines can **stifle** creativity if people never have time to explore.

drill.sentence: Too much homework can {{stifle}} a child's natural curiosity.
drill.hint: hold back so it can't grow (not *kill*, *crush*, *smother* or *squash*)

entries.related: *suppress* — deliberately prevent from being seen or expressed; *smother* — stop by covering, also figurative; *foster* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A confusing and difficult problem, often one where every possible choice has a downside.
entries.usage: Neutral to slightly formal, common in journalism and conversation: *face a conundrum*, *quite a conundrum*, *the conundrum of how to …*. It can be light and humorous for everyday dilemmas (*the eternal conundrum of what to cook*).
entries.pattern: face / pose a conundrum; the conundrum of how / whether to …
examples: Here's our **conundrum**: the cheaper apartment is bigger, but it's an hour from work.
For coaches, the **conundrum** is how to rest star players without losing games.
What to get my dad for his birthday is an annual **conundrum**, since he says he wants nothing.

drill.sentence: Whether Grandma should move in with us or into a nursing home is a real {{conundrum}} for our family.
drill.hint: puzzling situation with no easy answer (not *dilemma*, *quandary* or *challenge*)

entries.related: *dilemma* — a choice between two options, both bad; *quandary* — a state of not knowing what to do; *puzzle* — something hard to understand.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: One of the central principles or beliefs of a theory, movement, profession or organization.
entries.usage: Usually *a (central / core / basic) tenet of* + a system of ideas: *a core tenet of good design*. It is common in academic writing, journalism and serious discussion; in conversation, *principle* is more usual. Do not confuse it with *tenant*, a person who rents a home.
entries.pattern: a central / core / basic tenet of + system of ideas
examples: A basic **tenet** of good customer service is never to make people repeat themselves.
Innocent until proven guilty is a core **tenet** of the American legal system.
One **tenet** of my grandmother's cooking was that nothing should ever go to waste.

drill.sentence: "Leave no trace" is a central {{tenet}} of responsible camping: whatever you carry in, you carry out.
drill.hint: fundamental belief (formal, not *principle* or *pillar*)

mistake.wrong: Free speech is a basic tenant of democracy.
mistake.right: Free speech is a basic tenet of democracy.
mistake.why: A *tenant* rents a home; a principle is a *tenet*, with one *n* in the middle and a short final syllable.

entries.related: *principle* — the everyday word; *doctrine* — a set of official beliefs; *creed* — a set of beliefs, often religious.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To decide not to have or do something you would like, usually to save money or to gain something else.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and personal finance: *forgo a salary*, *forgo a vacation*, *forgo dessert*. The past forms *forwent* and *forgone* are rare, so people usually say *decided to forgo*. The spelling *forego* is also used, but careful writers keep it for *go before*, as in *a foregone conclusion*.
entries.pattern: forgo something (to do something); decide / choose to forgo something
examples: The founders agreed to **forgo** salaries for the first two years to keep the company alive.
We decided to **forgo** a big wedding and put the money toward a down payment.
Many patients **forgo** dental care because their insurance doesn't cover it.

drill.sentence: To save for our trip to Japan, we're {{forgoing}} restaurants and cooking at home every night.
drill.hint: choosing to do without (formal, not *skipping*, *avoiding* or *giving up*)

entries.related: *give up* — the everyday phrase; *do without* — manage without something; *waive* — formally give up a right or a fee.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not injured, damaged or harmed after a dangerous or difficult situation.
entries.usage: Almost always after verbs like *escape*, *emerge*, *come out*, *walk away* or *survive*: *escaped unscathed*. It is used for people, buildings and reputations, and is often limited with *relatively*, *largely* or *not entirely*. It normally comes after the verb, not before a noun.
entries.pattern: escape / emerge / walk away / come through (relatively) unscathed
examples: Both drivers walked away **unscathed**, even though the cars were totaled.
Our street came through the hurricane almost **unscathed**, while the next town lost dozens of homes.
Few companies emerged from the recession completely **unscathed**.

drill.sentence: Their cat fell from a third-floor balcony but somehow landed {{unscathed}} in the bushes.
drill.hint: not hurt in any way (not *unharmed*, *unhurt*, *uninjured* or *safely*)

entries.related: *unharmed* — plainer; *intact* — undamaged, about things; *scathing* — from the same old root, but it means *harshly critical*.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Dull and lacking energy, enthusiasm or quality; not impressive.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, sports reports and business news: *a lackluster performance*, *lackluster sales*, *a lackluster economy*. It suggests disappointment rather than total failure. *Lackluster* is the American spelling; British English writes *lacklustre*.
entries.pattern: a lackluster performance / season / response; lackluster sales / growth
examples: After a **lackluster** first half, the home team came back to win in overtime.
The food was **lackluster**, but the view of the bay made up for it.
The phone's **lackluster** sales forced the company to cut the price by a third.

drill.sentence: Her singing was fine, but the band's {{lackluster}} playing made the whole concert feel flat.
drill.hint: without energy or brilliance (not *dull*, *listless*, *lifeless* or *uninspired*)

entries.related: *mediocre* — of only average quality; *uninspired* — lacking new ideas; *stellar* — the opposite, excellent.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The responsibility or duty to do something, especially to prove something or to take action.
entries.usage: Almost always *the onus is on* + someone (*to do something*), or *put / place / shift the onus on* someone. It is common in legal, business and journalistic writing. In conversation, *it's up to* + someone is more natural.
entries.pattern: the onus is on someone (to do something); put / shift the onus on someone
examples: When you rent a car, the **onus** is on you to check for damage before you drive away.
The new law puts the **onus** on landlords to fix mold within thirty days.
Some apps shift the **onus** onto users by hiding important details in the terms and conditions.

drill.sentence: In a criminal trial, the {{onus}} is on the prosecution to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
drill.hint: duty to act or prove (short formal word, not *burden* or *responsibility*)

entries.related: *burden of proof* — the legal term; *responsibility* — the general word; *it's up to someone* — conversational.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A feeling of friendship, trust and loyalty among people who work, play or go through something together.
entries.usage: Common in talk about teams, coworkers, soldiers and classmates: *a sense of camaraderie*, *the camaraderie among the players*. It is warm and positive and usually describes a group, not just two people. People often name it as what they miss most after leaving a job or a team.
entries.pattern: a (strong) sense of camaraderie; the camaraderie among / between + group
examples: What I miss most about the restaurant job is the **camaraderie** in the kitchen after closing.
Long bus rides to away games built a real **camaraderie** among the players.
There's a special **camaraderie** among parents waiting outside the school in the rain.

drill.sentence: After three weeks on the hiking trail together, the group had developed a strong sense of {{camaraderie}}.
drill.hint: warm group loyalty and trust (not *community*, *belonging*, *fellowship* or *solidarity*)

entries.related: *solidarity* — unity in support of a shared cause; *fellowship* — friendly association, a bit old-fashioned; *esprit de corps* — formal, pride and loyalty in a group.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: According to what is claimed, although it has not been proven and may not be true.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and legal writing to mark a claim as unverified, often about where something comes from: *a video purportedly showing …*, *a letter purportedly written by …*. It sounds skeptical. For unproven crimes, *allegedly* is the usual word, and in conversation *supposedly* is more natural.
entries.pattern: purportedly + participle (written by, showing, from …)
examples: A letter **purportedly** written by Mark Twain turned up in an attic in Ohio.
The supplement **purportedly** boosts memory, but there's no good evidence that it works.
Police are examining a video **purportedly** showing the suspect near the scene.

drill.sentence: The online seller offered a jersey {{purportedly}} signed by the whole team, but it turned out to be fake.
drill.hint: as claimed, but unproven (not *supposedly*, *allegedly* or *reportedly*)

entries.related: *supposedly* — more conversational; *allegedly* — the usual word for unproven crimes; *ostensibly* — as stated, though the real reason is different.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To examine words or statements very closely to work out exactly what they mean, including any hidden meaning.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and educated speech: *parse someone's words / statement / comments*, especially when the statement is vague or carefully worded. *Parse every word* suggests very close, sometimes excessive, analysis. In grammar and computing, *parse* means to break a sentence or text into its parts.
entries.pattern: parse someone's words / statement / remarks / language
examples: Fans **parsed** every word of the coach's statement for hints about the quarterback's future.
Don't **parse** my texts so carefully; sometimes “OK” just means OK.
Lawyers spent hours **parsing** the contract to see who had to pay for the repairs.

drill.sentence: After their first date, she {{parsed}} his goodnight text for any sign that he wanted to see her again.
drill.hint: went over word by word for hidden meaning (not *analyzed*, *studied*, *read* or *scanned*)

entries.related: *scrutinize* — examine very carefully, more general; *read between the lines* — find a hidden meaning; *dissect* — analyze in great detail, often critically.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Freedom to act, decide or change things as you wish, within certain limits.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing about rules, deadlines, bosses and parents: *give someone leeway*, *have some leeway*, *a little leeway*. It is usually uncountable: *some leeway*, *a lot of leeway*, *a little leeway*. It is often followed by *in* + *how / what* or by *to* + verb.
entries.pattern: give / allow someone (some) leeway; leeway in how … / to do something
examples: My boss gives me a lot of **leeway** in how I organize my week.
The teacher allowed some **leeway** on the deadline because of the snowstorm.
We give our sixteen-year-old more **leeway** on weekends, as long as she texts us.

drill.sentence: The recipe is just a guide, so you have some {{leeway}} with the spices.
drill.hint: space to decide for yourself (not *flexibility*, *latitude*, *freedom* or *room*)

entries.related: *latitude* — more formal; *wiggle room* — informal, space to change a position; *flexibility* — willingness or ability to change.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something that is different from what is normal or expected, usually in an unwelcome way and usually only once.
entries.usage: Often used to dismiss a bad result as a one-time event: *the loss was an aberration*, *a statistical aberration*. It is common in sports, business, news and science writing. It also has technical meanings in optics and genetics.
entries.pattern: an aberration (from the norm); a statistical / temporary aberration
examples: The coach called the forty-point loss an **aberration** and promised it wouldn't happen again.
Economists expect prices to fall again and see last month's jump as a statistical **aberration**.
Apart from one strange **aberration** in college, when he dyed his hair green, my brother has always been very conventional.

drill.sentence: Mild winters used to be an {{aberration}} here, but now they seem to be the norm.
drill.hint: a departure from what's normal (not *exception*, *anomaly*, *outlier* or *rarity*)

entries.related: *anomaly* — something unusual, neutral, common in science; *fluke* — informal, a lucky or unlucky accident; *the norm* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In large amounts or very many times; very freely.
entries.usage: Mostly in a few fixed combinations: *apologize profusely*, *thank someone profusely*, *sweat profusely*, *bleed profusely*. It comes after the verb. With apologies and thanks, it can suggest a little too much.
entries.pattern: apologize / thank someone / sweat / bleed profusely
examples: The waiter spilled red wine on my shirt and apologized **profusely**.
By the time he got off the subway in August, he was sweating **profusely**.
The cut on her forehead was bleeding **profusely**, so we drove straight to the ER.

drill.sentence: When we returned her lost wallet, the woman thanked us {{profusely}} and insisted on buying us lunch.
drill.hint: very many times and very freely (not *repeatedly*, *warmly*, *effusively* or *endlessly*)

entries.related: *effusively* — with great, sometimes excessive enthusiasm; *profuse* — the adjective (*profuse apologies*); *sparingly* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: More than is reasonable, necessary or justified.
entries.usage: Very often in negatives: *not unduly worried / concerned / alarmed*. It is common in official statements, medical advice and legal writing (*unduly harsh*, *unduly influenced*). In conversation, *too* or *overly* is more natural, and the adjective is *undue* (*undue pressure*).
entries.pattern: not unduly + worried / concerned / alarmed; unduly harsh / influenced
examples: The doctor said the lump was probably harmless and that I shouldn't be **unduly** worried.
Critics said the sentence was **unduly** harsh for a first offense.
The coach doesn't seem **unduly** concerned about losing two starters to injury.

drill.sentence: The landlord promised that the repairs wouldn't {{unduly}} disturb the tenants.
drill.hint: more than is reasonable (formal, not *overly*, *unnecessarily* or *excessively*)

entries.related: *overly* — more common, before adjectives; *undue* — the adjective; *unnecessarily* — when there was no need at all.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Extremely and harshly critical, in a way that is meant to hurt.
entries.usage: Common in news, reviews and official reports: *a scathing review*, *a scathing report*, *scathing criticism*, *a scathing attack on* someone. It describes words, reviews and reports rather than people's character. The *th* is voiced, as in *this*.
entries.pattern: a scathing review / report / letter / attack (on someone)
examples: The restaurant closed a month after a **scathing** review in the local paper.
A **scathing** audit found that the city had wasted millions on snow removal contracts.
My sister wrote a **scathing** email to the airline after they lost her luggage twice.

drill.sentence: Critics were {{scathing}} about the remake, calling it lazy and pointless.
drill.hint: cuttingly harsh in judgment (not *brutal*, *harsh* or *savage*)

entries.related: *withering* — so critical it makes someone feel small (*a withering look*); *blistering* — very angry and harsh; *glowing* — the opposite (*a glowing review*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: No longer interested or excited, and somewhat cynical, because you have seen or done something too often.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and writing about work, cities, dating and entertainment: *a jaded New Yorker*, *jaded about dating*. It suggests lost enthusiasm rather than anger. Typical patterns are *jaded about* + topic and *jaded by* + experience.
entries.pattern: jaded about something; jaded by years of …; a jaded + person
examples: After ten years in the ER, she's a little **jaded**, but she still cares about every patient.
Even the most **jaded** New Yorkers stopped to watch the eclipse.
I've been on so many bad first dates that I'm getting **jaded** about the whole thing.

drill.sentence: Food critics can get so {{jaded}} that even a great meal barely impresses them.
drill.hint: worn out and unimpressed by too much experience (not *blasé*, *cynical* or *spoiled*)

entries.related: *cynical* — believing people act only from self-interest; *blasé* — unimpressed because you've seen it before; *disillusioned* — disappointed after learning the truth.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Meant to seem very impressive, but too ambitious, too elaborate or unrealistic.
entries.usage: Critical; used for plans, claims, ideas, buildings and language: *grandiose plans*, *grandiose claims*, *a grandiose vision*. It suggests that the ambition is bigger than the ability or the need. In psychology, it describes an exaggerated sense of one's own importance.
entries.pattern: grandiose plans / schemes / claims / ideas / language
examples: He had **grandiose** plans to open a chain of restaurants, but he never finished the first one.
The new town hall is a **grandiose** building with marble columns, which seems a bit much for a town of eight thousand.
My brother's toast was full of **grandiose** language about destiny, even though the couple had only been dating for eight months.

drill.sentence: Our neighbor has {{grandiose}} plans for his backyard: a pool, a waterfall and a tennis court.
drill.hint: impressive-sounding but unrealistic (not *grand*, *ambitious*, *lofty* or *elaborate*)

entries.related: *pretentious* — trying to seem more important or cultured than you are; *grand* — impressive, usually positive; *ambitious* — positive or neutral.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A situation in which the people involved cannot agree, so that no progress is possible.
entries.usage: Common in news about negotiations, contracts and disputes: *reach an impasse*, *break the impasse*, *the talks are at an impasse*. It is also used, a little formally, for disagreements at home. It is often followed by *over* + the issue.
entries.pattern: reach / break / end an impasse; be at an impasse (over something)
examples: Contract talks between the teachers and the school district have reached an **impasse**.
We were at an **impasse** over where to spend Thanksgiving, so we flipped a coin.
A mediator was brought in to break the **impasse** between the landlord and the tenants.

drill.sentence: Neither side would lower its price, so the sale of the house was stuck at an {{impasse}}.
drill.hint: a point where neither side will move

entries.related: *deadlock* — very similar, common in politics and law; *stalemate* — from chess, neither side can win; *breakthrough* — the end of an impasse.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: So high that it prevents people from buying, using or doing something.
entries.usage: Used for costs and prices, often to explain why something isn't done: *the cost is prohibitive*, *prohibitive prices*. The adverb is very frequent in *prohibitively expensive*. Common in news, business and everyday talk about money.
entries.pattern: a prohibitive cost / price; prohibitively expensive / high
examples: Many rural fire departments find the cost of a new engine **prohibitive**, so they buy used ones.
Shipping costs to Alaska can be **prohibitively** high, so many online stores won't deliver there at all.
The drug works, but its **prohibitive** price keeps it out of reach for most patients.

drill.sentence: We wanted to bring our dog on vacation, but the airline's pet fee was {{prohibitive}}, so she stayed with Grandma.
drill.hint: so high that it rules out the plan (not *exorbitant* or *steep*)

mistake.wrong: Smoking is prohibitive in the building.
mistake.right: Smoking is prohibited in the building.
mistake.why: *Prohibitive* describes a cost that stops people; for something that is not allowed, use *prohibited*.

entries.related: *exorbitant* — unreasonably high, stresses unfairness; *out of reach* — impossible to afford; *affordable* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To force someone out of a position of power or a job, often by a vote or after a struggle.
entries.usage: Very common in news headlines because it is short: *oust a CEO*, *ousted from power*, *ousted as chairman*. It is often passive (*was ousted*) and sounds journalistic; in conversation people say *push out* or *kick out*. The noun *ouster* is mainly American (*the CEO's ouster*).
entries.pattern: oust someone (from a position / as + title); be ousted (by the board / in a coup)
examples: The board voted to **oust** the CEO after a year of falling profits and bad press.
The army **ousted** the elected government and closed the airports.
Members of the book club **ousted** their organizer after she picked six thrillers in a row.

drill.sentence: Neighbors were so unhappy with the HOA president that they voted to {{oust}} him at the annual meeting.
drill.hint: force him out of the job (not *remove*, *replace*, *unseat* or *recall*)

entries.related: *depose* — remove a ruler, formal; *topple* — bring down a government or leader; *unseat* — remove from an elected position.
